In mathematics, a '''representation on coordinate rings''' is a [[representation of a group]] on coordinate rings of affine varieties.

Let ''X'' be an [[affine algebraic variety]] over an [[algebraically closed field]] ''k'' of [[characteristic (algebra)|characteristic]] zero with the action of a [[reductive algebraic group]] ''G''.<ref>''G'' is not assumed to be [[connected space|connected]] so that the results apply to finite groups.</ref> ''G'' then [[group action|acts]] on the coordinate ring <math>k[X]</math> of ''X'' as a [[left regular representation]]: <math>(g \cdot f)(x) = f(g^{-1} x)</math>. This is a representation of ''G'' on the coordinate ring of ''X''.

The most basic case is when ''X'' is an affine space (that is, ''X'' is a finite-dimensional representation of ''G'') and the coordinate ring is a [[polynomial ring]]. The most important case is when ''X'' is a [[symmetric variety]]; i.e., the quotient of ''G'' by a [[fixed-point subgroup]] of an involution.

== Isotypic decomposition ==
Let <math>k[X]_{(\lambda)}</math> be the sum of all ''G''-submodules of <math>k[X]</math> that are isomorphic to the [[simple module]] <math>V^{\lambda}</math>; it is called the <math>\lambda</math>-[[isotypic component]] of <math>k[X]</math>. Then there is a direct sum decomposition:
:<math>k[X] = \bigoplus_{\lambda} k[X]_{(\lambda)}</math>
where the sum runs over all simple ''G''-modules <math>V^{\lambda}</math>. The existence of the decomposition follows, for example, from the fact that the [[group ring|group algebra]] of ''G'' is semisimple since ''G'' is reductive.<!-- see [[algebra representation]]. -->

''X'' is called ''multiplicity-free'' (or [[spherical variety]]<ref>{{harvnb|Goodman|Wallach|2009|loc=Remark 12.2.2.}}</ref>) if every irreducible representation of ''G'' appears at most one time in the coordinate ring; i.e., <math>\operatorname{dim} k[X]_{(\lambda)} \le \operatorname{dim} V^{\lambda}</math>.
For example, <math>G</math> is multiplicity-free as <math>G \times G</math>-module. More precisely, given a closed subgroup ''H'' of ''G'', define
:<math>\phi_{\lambda}: V^{{\lambda}*} \otimes (V^{\lambda})^H \to k[G/H]_{(\lambda)}</math>
by setting <math>\phi_{\lambda}(\alpha \otimes v)(gH) = \langle \alpha, g \cdot v \rangle</math> and then extending <math>\phi_{\lambda}</math> by linearity. The functions in the image of <math>\phi_{\lambda}</math> are usually called [[matrix coefficient]]s. Then there is a direct sum decomposition of <math>G \times N</math>-modules (''N'' the normalizer of ''H'')
:<math>k[G/H] = \bigoplus_{\lambda} \phi_{\lambda}(V^{{\lambda}*} \otimes (V^{\lambda})^H)</math>,
which is an algebraic version of the [[Peter–Weyl theorem]] (and in fact the analytic version is an immediate consequence.) Proof: let ''W'' be a simple <math>G \times N</math>-submodules of <math>k[G/H]_{(\lambda)}</math>. We can assume <math>V^{\lambda} = W</math>. Let <math>\delta_1</math> be the [[linear functional]] of ''W'' such that <math>\delta_1(w) = w(1)</math>. Then <math>w(gH) = \phi_{\lambda}(\delta_1 \otimes w)(gH)</math>.
That is, the image of <math>\phi_{\lambda}</math> contains <math>k[G/H]_{(\lambda)}</math> and the opposite inclusion holds since <math>\phi_{\lambda}</math> is equivariant.

== Examples ==
*Let <math>v_{\lambda} \in V^{\lambda}</math> be a ''B''-[[eigenvector]] and ''X'' the closure of the orbit <math>G \cdot v_\lambda</math>. It is an affine variety called the highest weight vector variety by Vinberg–Popov. It is multiplicity-free.
